newsitem.title: USA: St.Petersburg calm before funeral of slain black.
newsitem.headline: St.Petersburg calm before funeral of slain black.

text.p: Police said Friday St. Petersburg was calm on the eve of the funeral of a black youth shot to death by a white policeman last week in an incident that ignited bloody race riots in the Florida city.
Rioting broke out in a poor black area last week after 18-year-old Tyron Lewis was killed by police. Eleven people were hurt and nearly 30 shops, homes or businesses torched in the violence.

Mayor David Fischer has said the funeral Saturday would be a "critical time" for the town. It was postponed until after Halloween, traditionally a bad night for police, but police spokeswoman Lilla Davis said Halloween had been calm this year. "All we had out last night were ghosts and goblins," she said.

A police spokesman, Bill Doniel, said the church and the funeral home had not asked for special police assistance, but he added, "We will certainly be in the neighbourhood with normal police service."
There has been no unrest since the riots last week, but tensions in the black community have mounted in recent days.

On Wednesday, a black militant group, the National People's Democratic Uhuru Movement, held a mock trial and declared the two police officers involved in the shooting guilty. They called for the immediate execution of the officers, the police chief, and Mayor Fischer.
Resentment has been further fuelled by the announcement that only one black will sit on the 18-strong grand jury that meets next Wednesday to decide whether to indict Knight.
While security has not been stepped up for the funeral, officers now ride through the south side of town four to a car and are quick to break up any disturbance.

Police officer James Knight shot Lewis at the wheel of his car after stopping him for speeding. Police say the car appeared to lunge forward in an effort by Lewis to run down Knight and his colleague.

A flurry of investigations has been launched by the state attorney's office and the Tampa offices of the FBI and the U.S. Attorney. The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights has already visited the city to talk to officials and residents.
Black community leaders say poverty, lack of jobs and bleak prospects for blacks in St.Petersburg created tensions that stoked the unrest in the otherwise sleepy, affluent city.

Saturday's service will include a eulogy delivered by Dr. Joseph Lowery, national president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. The SCLC office in St.Petersburg has called for an outside investigation into Lewis' death.
